title: API Strategy and Design for Government
objectives: Design APIs that enable interoperability and follow government standards
Apply the GDS API technical and data standards to real service architecture
Choose between API styles (REST, GraphQL, event-driven) for government use cases
Design APIs for multiple consumers with different needs
Version, document, and govern APIs throughout their lifecycle
whyThisMatters:
APIs are the integration fabric of modern government. Every interaction between services — within a department, across departments, with shared platforms like GOV.UK One Login, and with external partners — happens through APIs. The quality of your API design determines whether these interactions are reliable, performant, and maintainable, or whether they become the source of integration failures, versioning nightmares, and operational incidents.

The GDS API technical and data standards provide clear guidance for government API design. The UK's Digital Standards Strategy (2026-2030) reinforces the importance of technical standards for interoperability. The Open Standards Board selects mandatory standards for government. APIs designed to these standards work well across the government ecosystem. APIs that deviate create integration friction that multiplies with every consumer.

For solution architects, API design is not just a technical concern — it is a strategic one. Your APIs define what your service can do for others. They are contracts that, once published, constrain how you can evolve your service. A well-designed API enables an ecosystem of consumers you may not even have anticipated. A poorly-designed API becomes technical debt that every consumer inherits.

content.heading: The GDS API Technical and Data Standards
content.body:
The GDS API technical and data standards are the authoritative guide for designing, building, and operating APIs in government. Following them ensures your APIs work consistently across the government ecosystem and meets the Technology Code of Practice's principles of openness and interoperability.

Key standards include:

Use RESTful design principles. APIs should use HTTP methods semantically: GET for retrieval (safe, idempotent), POST for creation, PUT for full replacement, PATCH for partial update, DELETE for removal. Resources should be nouns, not verbs (/applications not /getApplications). Use plural resource names (/applications/123 not /application/123).

Use JSON as the default data format. JSON is the lingua franca of modern APIs and is well-supported by all platforms. Use camelCase for property names in JSON (matching JavaScript conventions). Include a Content-Type header of application/json.

Use HTTPS for all API communications. No exceptions. Even internal APIs should use HTTPS because network boundaries are not trust boundaries in modern cloud environments.

Use OAuth 2.0 for API authorisation. For service-to-service communication, use the client credentials grant. For user-facing APIs, use the authorisation code grant. Do not invent custom authorisation schemes.

Version your APIs. Use URL path versioning (/v1/applications) for major versions. Make breaking changes only in new major versions. Support the previous version for a defined deprecation period to give consumers time to migrate.

Document APIs using the OpenAPI Specification (formerly Swagger). Publish machine-readable API documentation that consumers can use to generate client code, validate requests, and understand the API without reading prose.

Use standard HTTP status codes consistently. 200 for success, 201 for created, 400 for bad request (client error), 401 for unauthorised, 403 for forbidden, 404 for not found, 429 for rate limited, 500 for server error. Do not use 200 with an error body.

Implement rate limiting to protect your service and be fair to all consumers. Return a 429 status code when limits are exceeded, with Retry-After header indicating when the consumer can try again.

Provide meaningful error responses. Include an error code, a human-readable message, and where possible, guidance on how to fix the problem. Do not expose internal implementation details in error messages (security risk).

content.heading: Choosing API Styles for Government Use Cases
content.body:
REST is the default standard for government APIs, but it is not the only option. Different styles suit different use cases.

REST APIs (the government default) are appropriate for: CRUD operations on resources (create/read/update/delete applications, cases, registrations), synchronous request-response interactions where the consumer needs an immediate answer, and public or widely-consumed APIs where simplicity and discoverability matter. REST's strength is simplicity and universality — every platform and language has excellent REST support.

Event-driven APIs (webhooks, message streams) are appropriate for: notifications of state changes (application submitted, decision made, payment processed), integration between loosely-coupled services where the consumer does not need an immediate response, and patterns where multiple consumers need to react to the same event. Event-driven architecture reduces coupling — the publisher does not need to know who is listening.

GraphQL APIs are appropriate for: situations where different consumers need different subsets of the same data (a mobile app needs a summary, a desktop app needs full detail, an API consumer needs specific fields), and complex data retrieval that would require many REST calls. GraphQL is not yet widely adopted in government — consider carefully whether the added complexity is justified. The GDS standards focus on REST.

Batch/file-based APIs are still appropriate for: bulk data transfers where real-time is not required (daily data extracts, monthly reporting), integration with legacy systems that cannot support real-time APIs, and large-volume data processing (uploading 100,000 records is better as a batch file than 100,000 individual API calls).

For most government services, REST APIs following the GDS standards are the right choice. Use event-driven patterns for asynchronous communication between your own services and for cross-government notifications. Consider GraphQL only if you have genuinely diverse consumer needs that REST cannot serve efficiently. Use batch for high-volume data exchange where real-time is not needed.

Document your choice as an ADR. If you deviate from the default (REST), explain why the alternative better serves your specific use case.

content.heading: Designing APIs for Multiple Consumers
content.body:
Government APIs often serve multiple consumer types with different needs. A grant service API might be consumed by: the citizen-facing web application, the internal caseworker tool, a management reporting dashboard, partner organisations checking grant status, and cross-government data sharing services. Each has different requirements for data volume, response time, authentication, and detail level.

Design principles for multi-consumer APIs:

Provide filtering and field selection. Allow consumers to request only the fields they need (sparse fieldsets) and filter results to relevant subsets. A mobile app requesting an application status needs only the status field, not the full application data. Returning minimal data reduces bandwidth, improves performance, and reduces the risk of exposing data a consumer does not need.

Use pagination for collections. Never return unbounded lists. Implement cursor-based or offset-based pagination with sensible default page sizes. A management dashboard querying all applications must not receive 500,000 records in a single response.

Separate read and write APIs where appropriate. Consumers who only read data (reporting, dashboards, partner queries) can be served by a read-optimised API backed by a read replica or cache. Consumers who create or update data need a write API that talks to the primary data store. This separation (CQRS pattern) prevents read-heavy consumers from competing with write operations for database resources.

Design for the consumer, not for your database. A common anti-pattern is designing APIs that mirror your database schema — exposing internal implementation details and forcing consumers to understand your data model. Instead, design APIs from the consumer's perspective: what data does this consumer need, in what shape, to accomplish their task?

Consider API products for different consumer categories. An internal API (consumed by your own frontend) can be less formally governed than a public API (consumed by external partners). You might offer: a private API (no external consumers, can change freely), a partner API (specific known consumers with agreed contracts), and a public API (discoverable by any government consumer, governed by the GDS standards).

content.heading: API Versioning and Lifecycle Management
content.body:
APIs are contracts. Once published, consumers depend on them. Changing an API without managing the impact on consumers breaks things — sometimes catastrophically, always annoyingly. API lifecycle management ensures your APIs evolve without causing consumer outages.

Versioning strategy: the GDS standards recommend URL path versioning (/v1/applications, /v2/applications). This makes the version explicit and allows consumers to migrate at their own pace. When you need to make a breaking change (removing a field, changing a field type, restructuring a response), release it in a new major version while continuing to support the previous version.

What constitutes a breaking change: removing a field or endpoint, changing a field's data type, making a previously optional field required, changing the semantics of a field (same name, different meaning), or changing an error response format. Non-breaking changes (adding new optional fields, adding new endpoints, adding new optional parameters) can be made within the same version.

Deprecation policy: when you release a new version, provide a clear deprecation timeline for the old version. Government APIs should support the previous version for at least 6 months — longer for widely-consumed APIs. Communicate the deprecation clearly: update the API documentation, return deprecation headers in responses, and contact known consumers directly.

API discovery and documentation: publish your APIs in a discoverable location. The government API catalogue exists for this purpose. Maintain up-to-date OpenAPI specifications that consumers can rely on. Documentation should include: getting started guide, authentication instructions, endpoint reference, error code reference, rate limit information, and example requests and responses.

API governance: for APIs consumed externally (by other departments or partners), establish a governance process for changes. This might be as simple as: propose the change, assess consumer impact, communicate with affected consumers, implement with deprecation of the old version, and support the old version until the deprecation period expires. Include API changes in your Design Authority reviews where they affect external consumers.

content.heading: Security and Access Control for Government APIs
content.body:
API security in government must be proportionate to the data classification and the consumer type. An API serving publicly available data requires different security from one serving OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE personal data.

Authentication (proving who you are):

For service-to-service APIs (machine-to-machine): use OAuth 2.0 client credentials grant. Each consumer service has a client ID and secret (or certificate-based credential) that it uses to obtain an access token. The token is short-lived and must be refreshed.

For user-facing APIs (accessed on behalf of a citizen): use OAuth 2.0 authorisation code grant, typically via GOV.UK One Login for citizen-facing services. The citizen authenticates with One Login, which issues a token that your API validates.

For partner APIs (external organisations): use mutual TLS (mTLS) for transport security plus OAuth 2.0 for authorisation. The certificate provides transport-level authentication; the OAuth token provides application-level authorisation.

Authorisation (proving what you are allowed to do):

Implement least-privilege access: consumers should have access only to the specific resources and operations they need. A reporting consumer needs read access to aggregated data, not write access to individual records. A partner checking application status needs access to their applications only, not all applications.

Use scopes in OAuth tokens to limit what each consumer can access. Define granular scopes (read:applications, write:applications, read:decisions) and grant each consumer only the scopes they need.

For APIs serving personal data: validate that the requesting user or service has a legitimate basis for accessing the specific data requested. This may require checking the relationship between the requester and the data subject — a solicitor can access their client's case data but not other cases.

Rate limiting and abuse protection:

Implement rate limiting per consumer to prevent any single consumer from overwhelming the service. Rate limits should be generous enough for legitimate use but restrictive enough to prevent abuse. Return clear 429 responses with Retry-After headers. Monitor for unusual patterns that might indicate credential compromise or automated abuse.

Input validation:

Validate all inputs at the API boundary. Do not trust consumer-supplied data. Check types, ranges, formats, and sizes. Reject malformed requests with clear 400 responses that explain what was wrong without revealing internal implementation details. This prevents injection attacks, buffer overflows, and data corruption.

content.heading: API-First Design and Government Platform Integration
content.body:
API-first design means defining the API contract before implementing the service behind it. This approach has significant benefits for government services that will be consumed by multiple clients or integrated with government platforms.

Define the OpenAPI specification first. Write the API contract (endpoints, request/response schemas, error formats) before writing implementation code. This allows: frontend and backend teams to work in parallel (the frontend codes against the contract using mocks), consumers to begin integration planning immediately, and automated testing to validate the implementation against the contract.

Design for platform integration from day one. If your service will use GOV.UK One Login, design your API to accept and validate One Login tokens. If your service will send notifications via GOV.UK Notify, design the API event model to trigger notifications at appropriate points. If your service will accept payments via GOV.UK Pay, design the payment flow to accommodate Pay's callback pattern.

Register your API for government discovery. The government maintains an API catalogue where departments can find and consume each other's APIs. Publishing your API there makes it discoverable for cross-government reuse — fulfilling the Technology Code of Practice's share and reuse principle.

Design for the government API ecosystem. Follow conventions that are consistent with other government APIs so that consumers who have integrated with one government API find yours familiar. Consistent patterns for pagination, error handling, authentication, and resource naming reduce the learning curve for each new integration.

Consider API management platforms. For APIs with multiple consumers, rate limiting requirements, and analytics needs, an API management platform (API gateway) provides: centralised authentication and authorisation, rate limiting and throttling, request/response transformation, analytics and monitoring, and developer portal for documentation and onboarding. Most cloud providers offer managed API gateway services that meet government security requirements.

workedExample.title: Designing the API Strategy for a DESNZ Regulatory Reporting Platform
workedExample.context: DESNZ is building a new regulatory reporting platform that will receive compliance data from 5,000 energy companies, provide data to 3 internal teams (compliance, enforcement, policy analysis), share data with Ofgem (the regulator), and expose selected aggregated data publicly for transparency. The platform replaces a legacy system that accepted data via email attachments and manual spreadsheet processing.
workedExample.approach:
The Solution Architect designs an API-first platform with distinct APIs for each consumer category.

API 1 — Submission API (external companies):
Purpose: Energy companies submit compliance reports.
Style: REST, following GDS standards.
Auth: OAuth 2.0 with client credentials (companies register for API credentials).
Key endpoints: POST /v1/submissions (upload report), GET /v1/submissions/{id}/status (check processing status), GET /v1/submissions (list own submissions with filtering).
Design decisions: accept JSON for structured data and multipart for file attachments. Validate against regulatory schema on receipt. Return 202 Accepted (processing is async). Provide webhook notification when processing completes.

API 2 — Internal API (caseworkers and analysts):
Purpose: Internal teams query and manage compliance data.
Style: REST with expanded filtering and search capabilities.
Auth: OAuth 2.0 via departmental identity provider (SAML federation).
Key endpoints: GET /internal/v1/submissions (search with complex filters), GET /internal/v1/companies/{id}/compliance-history, POST /internal/v1/submissions/{id}/assessment (record compliance assessment).
Design decisions: support rich filtering (date range, company size, sector, compliance status). Pagination with cursor-based navigation. Separate read and write paths (reads from replica).

API 3 — Partner API (Ofgem):
Purpose: Ofgem receives compliance data for their regulatory functions.
Style: REST with mutual TLS.
Auth: mTLS + OAuth 2.0 with specific Ofgem scopes.
Key endpoints: GET /partner/v1/submissions (filtered by Ofgem's regulatory scope), webhook notifications for new submissions in Ofgem's jurisdiction.
Design decisions: data minimisation — only expose fields Ofgem has legal basis to access. Rate limited. Formal SLA (99.9% availability, <2s response).

API 4 — Public API (transparency data):
Purpose: Public access to aggregated compliance statistics.
Style: REST, read-only, no authentication required.
Key endpoints: GET /public/v1/statistics/by-sector, GET /public/v1/statistics/by-region.
Design decisions: only aggregated data (no individual company data). Cached aggressively (hourly refresh). Rate limited per IP. OpenAPI specification published for any consumer.

Cross-cutting decisions (recorded as ADRs):
- ADR-001: REST API style for all APIs (standard, well-supported, aligns with GDS standards)
- ADR-002: URL path versioning (/v1/) with 12-month deprecation window for major versions
- ADR-003: Async processing for submissions (202 Accepted pattern with webhook notification)
- ADR-004: Separate internal and external API surfaces (different security models, different data exposure)
workedExample.outcome: The platform launches with all four APIs. 4,200 of 5,000 companies successfully onboard to the submission API within 6 months (the remainder continue using a transitional email route). Ofgem integrates within 3 months and decommissions their manual data request process. The public API is used by 15 external organisations including academic researchers and industry bodies — demonstrating cross-government data transparency without any additional development effort.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: Designing separate API products for each consumer category (external companies, internal teams, partner regulators, public) avoided the common problem of a single API trying to serve all needs and satisfying none. The async submission pattern (202 Accepted) was essential — processing a compliance report involves validation, schema checking, and cross-referencing that takes 30-60 seconds. Making this synchronous would have created unacceptable response times. Publishing the public API unlocked value the team had not anticipated — external researchers using the data for academic analysis that fed back into policy development.

civilServiceScenario.title: The API Breaking Change That Broke 12 Services
civilServiceScenario.background: A shared departmental API that provides business registration data is consumed by 12 internal services. The API team deployed a 'minor improvement' that renamed a field from 'companyName' to 'registeredName' (they considered this a correction rather than a breaking change). The deployment happened on a Friday afternoon without consumer notification. By Monday morning, 8 of the 12 consuming services had errors — some silently dropping the renamed field, others throwing exceptions. One service (a ministerial dashboard) showed blank company names for all records, which was noticed by the minister's private office.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: As the departmental Lead Solution Architect, you must: (1) resolve the immediate crisis, (2) determine responsibility, and (3) establish API governance that prevents recurrence.
constraints: Twelve services are affected — some are aware of the problem, some are not
The renamed field is now in production and reverting would affect consumers who have already updated
The minister's private office is asking why the dashboard is broken
The API team believes they improved the API and did nothing wrong
No formal API versioning or deprecation policy exists
No API consumer registry exists — the team did not know all consumers
Consuming teams have varying technical capability to respond quickly
The department has no API governance forum or standards
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Lead Solution Architect responsible for establishing API governance and resolving this incident.
civilServiceScenario.discussion:
This scenario illustrates what happens without API governance. The immediate fix is pragmatic: add the old field name back as an alias (both 'companyName' and 'registeredName' return the same data), notify all consumers of the situation, and plan a proper versioned migration for the future.

The governance gaps to address: establish that renaming a field IS a breaking change (regardless of intent), implement URL path versioning (the next breaking change goes in /v2/), create an API consumer registry (every consumer must register so they can be notified of changes), establish a deprecation policy (old versions supported for 6 months minimum with consumer notification), and create an API change review process (breaking changes reviewed by the Lead Architect before deployment). An ADR should record these governance decisions, and the API standards should be aligned with the GDS technical and data standards.

practiceArtefact.description: Design the API specification (in OpenAPI/prose format) for a government service that manages energy performance certificates (EPCs). The API must support: energy assessors uploading assessment results, property owners retrieving their certificates, estate agents querying ratings for multiple properties, and local authorities checking compliance by geographic area. Follow GDS API standards.
practiceArtefact.guidance: Define: resource naming, HTTP methods, URL structure, authentication per consumer type, pagination approach, error response format, and rate limiting. Show at least 4 key endpoints in detail. Consider how different consumers need different levels of access to the same underlying data.
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**API Design: Energy Performance Certificate Service**

Base URL: https://api.epc.desnz.gov.uk
Version: /v1/
Format: JSON (application/json)
Authentication: OAuth 2.0 (method varies by consumer type)
Documentation: OpenAPI 3.0 published at /v1/openapi.json

**Endpoints:**

1. POST /v1/assessments
Purpose: Energy assessor submits a new assessment
Auth: OAuth 2.0 client credentials (assessor organisation credential)
Request body: assessment data (property address, ratings, recommendations)
Response: 201 Created with Location header pointing to the created resource
Rate limit: 100 requests/minute per assessor organisation

2. GET /v1/certificates/{uprn}
Purpose: Retrieve the current EPC for a property by UPRN (Unique Property Reference Number)
Auth: None required (EPC data is public)
Response: 200 OK with certificate data (rating, valid-until date, recommendations)
Cache: CDN-cached for 24 hours (certificates change infrequently)
Rate limit: 1000 requests/minute per IP (public API)

3. GET /v1/certificates?uprns={uprn1,uprn2,...}&fields=rating,validUntil
Purpose: Bulk retrieval for estate agents (multiple properties, sparse fields)
Auth: OAuth 2.0 client credentials (registered estate agent credential)
Response: 200 OK with array of certificate summaries
Pagination: max 100 UPRNs per request
Rate limit: 500 requests/minute per estate agent

4. GET /v1/certificates?postcode-area={area}&rating-below={band}&page={n}
Purpose: Local authority compliance query (properties below required standard)
Auth: OAuth 2.0 client credentials (local authority credential with compliance scope)
Response: 200 OK with paginated results (20 per page, cursor-based)
Rate limit: 200 requests/minute per authority

**Error Format (all endpoints):**
```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR",
    "message": "The UPRN provided is not a valid format",
    "details": [{"field": "uprn", "issue": "Must be a 12-digit numeric value"}]
  }
}
```

**Standard HTTP Status Codes:**
200 OK, 201 Created, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorised, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests, 500 Internal Server Error

**Versioning:** URL path (/v1/). Breaking changes in /v2/ with 12-month v1 support.

**Rate Limit Headers:** X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset

reflectiveQuestions: How many APIs does your department expose to external consumers? Are they documented to GDS standards? Could a new consumer integrate without contacting your team?
Have you ever experienced an API breaking change that affected your service? How was it communicated, and how much notice did you receive?
Does your department have an API governance process? If someone wanted to publish a new API, what would they need to do?
Think about an API you consume from another department or platform. What would you change about its design if you could? What principles does your critique reflect?
How do you balance API stability (never breaking consumers) with API evolution (improving the API based on learning)? Where does your current practice fall on that spectrum?

knowledgeCheck.question: According to GDS API standards, what is the default data format for government APIs?
options: XML with SOAP wrappers
JSON with RESTful design principles
CSV for all data exchange
Protocol Buffers for maximum efficiency
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The GDS API technical and data standards specify JSON as the default format with RESTful design principles. REST with JSON is the government default because it is simple, widely supported, and consistent with the broader web ecosystem.

knowledgeCheck.question: What constitutes a breaking change in an API?
options: Adding a new optional field to a response
Adding a new endpoint
Removing or renaming an existing field, or changing a field's data type
Improving the response time of an endpoint
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Breaking changes are modifications that can cause existing consumers to fail: removing fields, renaming fields, changing data types, making optional fields required, or removing endpoints. Adding new optional fields, new endpoints, or new optional parameters are non-breaking changes that can be made within the same version.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why should government APIs implement rate limiting?
options: To artificially slow down external consumers for competitive advantage
To protect the service from overload and ensure fair access for all consumers
To generate revenue from API usage
Rate limiting is not recommended for government APIs
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Rate limiting protects the service from being overwhelmed by any single consumer (whether through legitimate high usage or abuse) and ensures fair access for all consumers. Government APIs should return 429 status codes with Retry-After headers when limits are exceeded.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the recommended approach for API versioning in government?
options: No versioning — APIs should never change
URL path versioning (/v1/, /v2/) with a defined deprecation period for old versions
Header-based versioning that is invisible in the URL
Date-based versioning using the deployment date
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The GDS standards recommend URL path versioning (/v1/applications). This makes the version explicit and allows consumers to migrate at their own pace. Old versions should be supported for a defined deprecation period (at least 6 months) to give consumers time to update their integrations.

knowledgeCheck.question: When designing an API consumed by multiple types of government user, what is the key design principle?
options: Build a single API endpoint that returns all possible data for all consumers
Build separate API surfaces for different consumer types with appropriate data exposure and access control
Let each consumer access the database directly for maximum flexibility
Design the API to mirror your database schema exactly
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Different consumers (citizens, internal staff, partner organisations, public transparency) need different data, different security models, and different performance characteristics. Separate API surfaces allow appropriate data exposure, access control, and optimisation for each consumer type rather than forcing a one-size-fits-all approach.
